5.t: Working with data: curvature over time
q: Calculate the mean rate of bending in the first 12 hours with light from one side.
26 / 12 = 2.2 degrees per hour.
Explain why the group lit from above is needed.
It is a control: it shows that the bending is caused by one-sided light, not by growth alone or by handling the seedlings.
Explain the result when the tip is covered.
The tip detects the light (phototropin receptors). Covered, it cannot detect the direction, so auxin is not moved and the shoot does not bend.
Explain how light from one side causes bending towards the light.
Auxin is moved to the shaded side (efflux carriers change position). Cells there elongate more (acid growth), so the shaded side grows longer and the shoot bends towards the light.
Suggest why bending slows after about 12 hours.
The tip now points towards the light, so both sides are lit more equally and auxin evens out.

14.t: Working with data: auxin and curvature
q: Describe the relationship between auxin concentration and curvature.
Curvature rises steeply to about 19 degrees at 0.2, peaks at about 20 degrees near 0.3–0.4, then falls at higher concentrations (5 degrees at 1.6).
Explain why the shoots bend away from the side with the block.
Auxin diffuses down that side, so its cells elongate more than those on the other side.
Explain why a block with no auxin is included.
It is a control: it shows that agar or cutting alone causes no bending.
Suggest why curvature falls at the highest concentrations.
Very high auxin inhibits elongation (for example by triggering ethylene production), so growth on that side is slowed.
A block from the shaded side of a lit shoot gave 15 degrees, one from the lit side 8 degrees. Estimate both concentrations and comment.

Using the rising part of the curve: shaded about 0.13, lit about 0.07 mg dm⁻³: about twice as much auxin on the shaded side. But 15 degrees could also mean about 0.7 on the falling part, so a dilution should be tested to be sure.

23.t: Working with data: ripening in a bag
q: Explain the effect of the banana.
A ripe banana releases ethylene; the higher concentration (6 ppm) triggers ripening sooner (5 days instead of 9).
The bag with banana and absorber ripened more slowly than tomatoes alone. Explain.
The absorber removed the banana’s ethylene and the tomatoes’ own (0.1 ppm, against 1.5 ppm), so there was less ethylene than in the bag with tomatoes alone.
Explain why the tomatoes ripened faster in a sealed bag than in an open tray.
Their own ethylene builds up in the bag. Ethylene makes the fruit produce even more ethylene: positive feedback.
Suggest why the bag at 10 °C was slowest of all.
The enzymes that make ethylene and soften the fruit work slowly at low temperature, so less ethylene is made (0.4 ppm).
Explain how a supplier could use these results to ship tomatoes a long way.
Pick them green, ship them cold with ethylene absorbers or good ventilation, then expose them to ethylene gas when they arrive.
